response.title: Is a big battery backup system cheaper than a whole-house standby generator if we lose power two or three times a year?
response.answer:
If you lose power only 2–3 times a year, a home battery backup can be cheaper than a whole-house standby generator—but it depends heavily on how long those outages last and how much of your house you want to power.

The biggest distinction is:

Battery backup: Often better for short outages (a few hours), especially if you only need essential appliances.

Standby generator: Usually more economical for long outages (24–72+ hours), particularly if you want to run the entire house, including air conditioning.

Battery + solar: Potentially attractive if you also want to reduce electricity bills, not just protect against outages.

+1

In this example, the generator is about $8,750 cheaper over 15 years. However, a battery that saves $600 per year through time-of-use electricity management would offset $9,000 of that difference.

My recommendation

For only 2–3 outages annually:

If outages last 1–6 hours, consider one battery for essential loads.

If outages last 6–24 hours, compare two batteries against a standby generator.

If outages regularly exceed 24 hours, favor a standby generator unless you have substantial solar generation.

The key is that a generator provides continuous energy, while a battery provides a fixed amount of stored energy. A 20 kW generator and a 20 kWh battery are not equivalent.

Three questions that would change my recommendation

How long do your outages typically last? Two hours, eight hours, or multiple days?

Do you already have solar panels? This can dramatically change the economics.

Do you want to power the entire house, including air conditioning, or just essentials?

With those three answers, I can estimate which option would cost less over 10–15 years for your situation.

- **Battery + solar:** Potentially attractive if you also want to reduce electricity bills, not just protect against outages.

## Typical installed cost comparison

These are approximate U.S. residential prices, including equipment and installation.

| System | Installed cost | Best use |
|---|---:|---|
| One 13.5 kWh battery | $12,000–$19,000 | Essential appliances |
| Two batteries (27 kWh) | $23,000–$31,000 | Most household loads |
| Three batteries (40.5 kWh) | $33,000–$44,000 | Larger whole-home backup |
| 20–24 kW standby generator | $9,000–$17,000 | Whole house, extended outages |

<caption>Approximate 2026 prices; battery figures reflect California estimates. Actual quotes vary with electrical and gas infrastructure. <Cite refs={["turn203400search2","turn203400search1","turn203400search4"]}/></caption>

## How long would the battery last?

Assume you install a 27 kWh battery system, with approximately 25 kWh available after allowing for losses and reserves.

{@body const [load,setLoad] = DIL.useState("1")}
{@body const [capacity,setCapacity] = DIL.useState("25")}
{@body const hours = Number(capacity)/Number(load)}
<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <text weight="medium">Battery backup runtime calculator</text>
  <box gap={1}>
    <label>Battery capacity</label>
    <radio-group direction="col" value={capacity} onChange={setCapacity}>
      <radio value="12.5">One battery — 12.5 kWh usable</radio>
      <radio value="25">Two batteries — 25 kWh usable</radio>
      <radio value="37.5">Three batteries — 37.5 kWh usable</radio>
    </radio-group>
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box gap={1}>
    <label>Average electricity consumption during outage</label>
    <radio-group direction="col" value={load} onChange={setLoad}>
      <radio value="0.5">0.5 kW — essentials only</radio>
      <radio value="1">1 kW — modest household use</radio>
      <radio value="2">2 kW — typical household with some HVAC</radio>
      <radio value="4">4 kW — heavy usage / air conditioning</radio>
    </radio-group>
  </box>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">Estimated backup duration</text>
    <title size="2xl" color="default" tabularNums>{hours>=24 ? `${(hours/24).toFixed(1)} days` : `${hours.toFixed(1)} hours`}</title>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Without solar recharging</text>
  </box>
</box>

## What about maintenance over 15 years?

Suppose you experience three outages annually, each lasting six hours.

| Expense over 15 years | Battery (2 units) | Generator |
|---|---:|---:|
| Initial installation | $27,000 | $13,000 |
| Routine maintenance | Minimal | ~$4,500 |
| Outage fuel | $0 | ~$750 |
| Estimated total | ~$27,000 | ~$18,250 |

These are illustrative calculations, excluding financing, electricity used to charge batteries, battery degradation, major repairs, replacement, and electricity-bill savings. Generator maintenance plans commonly cost several hundred dollars annually. <Cite refs={["turn203400search6","turn203400search3"]}/>

**In this example, the generator is about $8,750 cheaper over 15 years.** However, a battery that saves $600 per year through time-of-use electricity management would offset $9,000 of that difference.

## My recommendation

For only 2–3 outages annually:

- If outages last 1–6 hours, consider one battery for essential loads.
- If outages last 6–24 hours, compare two batteries against a standby generator.
- If outages regularly exceed 24 hours, favor a standby generator unless you have substantial solar generation.

The key is that a generator provides continuous energy, while a battery provides a fixed amount of stored energy. A 20 kW generator and a 20 kWh battery are not equivalent.

## Three questions that would change my recommendation

1. **How long do your outages typically last?** Two hours, eight hours, or multiple days?
2. **Do you already have solar panels?** This can dramatically change the economics.
3. **Do you want to power the entire house, including air conditioning, or just essentials?**

With those three answers, I can estimate which option would cost less over 10–15 years for your situation.
